query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using the CALPHAD method to design high-entropy alloys (HEAs) will lead to improved phase stability, refined microstructure, and optimized properties compared to alloys developed without such computational guidance.
generation.material_initial_state: HEAs with a broad compositional space where multiple phases (including undesired intermetallics) may form in conventional design routes.
generation.intervention: Application of the CALPHAD-based design strategy (in combination with data mining and multi-objective optimization) to screen alloy compositions and guide processing parameters.
generation.conditions: Within the typical HEA composition ranges (e.g., quinary systems such as Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti) and using available computational software and databases under controlled experimental synthesis conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced phase distribution with a dominant solid-liquid solution phase and reduced secondary intermetallic phases leading to a more homogeneous microstructure.
generation.mechanism: CALPHAD predicts thermodynamic parameters (e.g., mixing enthalpy, mixing entropy, atomic size difference, and omega parameter) that guide the selection of compositions favoring single-phase stability. This predictive capability informs processing conditions that refine microstructure and optimize mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The CALPHAD-designed HEAs will exhibit a single solid-solution phase with fewer secondary phases, resulting in improved mechanical performance and microstructural homogeneity relative to conventionally developed alloys.
generation.baseline: Alloys developed by trial-and-error methods or without guided thermodynamic predictions, often showing mixed phase structures and less optimized properties.
generation.boundary: The benefits of the CALPHAD method may be limited by the accuracy and completeness of the underlying thermodynamic databases and may require further experimental validation especially when kinetic factors dominate phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: While the trend toward improved phase stability and property optimization is expected, the precise magnitude of improvement in actual mechanical properties and microstructural refinement is uncertain until rigorously validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA samples: one set designed using the CALPHAD method (with computational predictions guiding alloy composition and processing parameters) and a control set developed by conventional methods. Process both groups under identical synthesis and heat-treatment conditions. Analyze phase composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties using standardized techniques.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification and quantification
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for microstructural imaging
Mechanical testing (such as tensile or compressive tests) for assessing strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CALPHAD-designed alloy samples do not show statistically significant improvements in phase stability (single-phase purity), microstructural homogeneity, and mechanical properties compared to the control group, the hypothesis that using CALPHAD enhances these outcomes is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
